newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASEAN to embark on serious Cambodian mediation.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN to embark on serious Cambodian mediation.

text.p: ASEAN has agreed to embark on a complex and far-reaching mediation effort to restore stability in Cambodia by paving the way for acceptable elections, sources close to the decision said on Tuesday.
"The target is elections on schedule in May (1998) with international monitors, with everyone participating and which can be seen as free and fair," said one source.

The sources, who asked not to be identified, said the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) accepted that it had taken on a huge task by its decision, made at a foreign ministers' meeting in Singapore on Monday.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen controls most of Cambodia. First prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, ousted in bloody fighting last month, is abroad with many of his FUNCINPEC party leaders. The two sides are still battling in the northwest.
Ranariddh begged ASEAN foreign ministers to ignore his replacement by FUNCINPEC, Foreign Minister Ung Huot.
Hun Sen has never been more than lukewarm to the idea of mediation by the nine-member ASEAN, which postponed Cambodia's entry following the fighting in Phnom Penh.
King Sihanouk has endorsed his son's replacement as first prime minister. He has also railed against it and threatened to abdicate in protest, though few believe he will do so.
"But there are positive signs in that there are some efforts in Phnom Penh to reform and reorganise institutions to make decent elections possible," said another source.

The sources said two critical elements of the ASEAN mediation effort were the depoliticisation of the military and police, now largely loyal to Hun Sen, and the disbanding of an 18,000-strong militia that runs the countryside on his behalf.
One proposal would bar soldiers and policemen from voting for 10 years, they said.
"The point is to reduce intimidation at the local level and give everyone a chance to express themselves in an election," said one source.

"No one expects a perfect election in a country that has been in chaos for 30 years, but an acceptable election will open the door for better things down the road, and that's what ASEAN wants," he said.
ASEAN agreed on Monday that its campaign would open with Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn talking to Ranariddh and Indonesian foreign minister Ali Alatas talking to Hun Sen and Ung Huot.
"They'll be looking for common ground on which the two Cambodian sides can meet and then take it from there. The plan is pretty flexible," one source said.
The sources said Hun Sen seemed amenable to moving in the direction ASEAN desired, despite earlier antagonism, partly because he desires international respectability.

"He also needs the money," one source said of the foreign aid that supplies about half the Cambodian government's budget and which has been under threat from Western countries upset by what they see as a Hun Sen coup.

But ASEAN, despite a public statement on Monday that Cambodia's membership -- alongside Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- was only a matter of time, it had set no target date.
"It all depends on what happens over the next few months, whether the talks progress," said one source.
There had been serious pressure from some ASEAN members, notably Malaysia and Vietnam, to get Cambodia into the organisation soon, the sources said.
"But they talked it through (on Monday) and all agreed that principles came first, that ASEAN couldn't accept a fait accompli in Phnom Penh. That would set a very bad precedent," one source said.

"There was also concern about letting in a country without political stability and the ability to maintain a policy of decision by consensus. Cambodia as it is now might well severely disrupt ASEAN's functioning," he added.
"This is also a chance for ASEAN to show in its 30th year that it is a mature organisation which can take on a very difficult matter and emerge with distinction."
